Linear Transform: A function that maps vectors from one vector space to another, satisfying $T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v)$ and $T(cu) = cT(u)$ for all vectors $u$, $v$ and scalars $c$.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 5><L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 6>

Matrix Transposition: An operation that swaps the rows and columns of a matrix.  The transpose of matrix $A$ is denoted as $A^T$.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 16>
Derivative: A measure of how a function changes with respect to a change in its input. <L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 21>

\textbf{Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for Image/Video Recognition<L[09L1-cnn] 2>}: A type of artificial neural network designed to process data with a grid-like topology, such as images.  CNNs use convolutional layers to extract features from the input data and pooling layers to reduce the dimensionality of the data. <L[09L1-cnn] 2>
\textbf{ImageNet Top-5 Classification Accuracy<L[09L1-cnn] 3>}: A metric used to evaluate the performance of image classification models on the ImageNet dataset.  It measures the percentage of times the correct class is among the top 5 predicted classes. <L[09L1-cnn] 3>
\textbf{AlexNet<L[09L1-cnn] 3>}: One of the first deep convolutional neural networks to achieve high accuracy in image classification, particularly on the ImageNet dataset.  It was notable for its use of GPUs for faster training. <L[09L1-cnn] 3>
\textbf{Dense Neural Network<L[09L1-cnn] 4>}: A type of artificial neural network where each neuron in one layer is connected to every neuron in the next layer.  This creates a fully connected network. <L[09L1-cnn] 4>
\textbf{Convolutional Neural Network (ConvNet)<L[09L1-cnn] 4>}: A type of artificial neural network that uses convolutional layers to extract features from input data, typically images.  It processes data in three dimensions (width, height, depth). <L[09L1-cnn] 4>
\textbf{Activation Function<L[09L1-cnn] 5>}: A non-linear function applied to the output of a neuron to introduce non-linearity into the network.  Examples include sigmoid and ReLU. <L[09L1-cnn] 5>
\textbf{Convolution Layer<L[09L1-cnn] 6>}: A layer in a convolutional neural network that applies a filter (kernel) to the input data to extract features.  The filter slides across the input data, performing element-wise multiplication and summation. <L[09L1-cnn] 6>
\textbf{Pooling Layer<L[09L1-cnn] 6>}: A layer in a convolutional neural network that reduces the spatial dimensions of the feature maps, typically by applying a max or average pooling operation. <L[09L1-cnn] 6>
\textbf{Convolution Filter<L[09L1-cnn] 7>}: A small matrix of weights used in a convolutional layer to extract features from the input data.  It slides across the input data, performing element-wise multiplication and summation. <L[09L1-cnn] 7>
\textbf{Input Map<L[09L1-cnn] 7>}: A matrix representing a portion of an image or a feature map from a previous layer in a convolutional neural network.  It serves as the input to a convolutional layer. <L[09L1-cnn] 7>
\textbf{Output Map<L[09L1-cnn] 7>}: A matrix representing the output of a convolutional layer.  It contains the extracted features from the input map. <L[09L1-cnn] 7>
\textbf{Zero Padding<L[09L1-cnn] 7>}: A technique used in convolutional neural networks to add zeros around the borders of the input data, maintaining the dimensions of the output feature maps. <L[09L1-cnn] 7>
\textbf{Multidimensional Convolution<L[09L1-cnn] 8><L[09L1-cnn] 9><L[09L1-cnn] 19>}: A convolution operation applied to input data with multiple channels (e.g., RGB channels in an image).  Each channel is processed independently by a corresponding filter. <L[09L1-cnn] 8><L[09L1-cnn] 9><L[09L1-cnn] 19>
\textbf{Local Receptive Field<L[09L1-cnn] 10><L[09L1-cnn] 11>}: The small region of the input data that a neuron in a convolutional layer is connected to.  This leads to sparse connectivity. <L[09L1-cnn] 10><L[09L1-cnn] 11>
\textbf{Sparse Connectivity<L[09L1-cnn] 10><L[09L1-cnn] 11><L[09L1-cnn] 12>}: A characteristic of convolutional neural networks where each neuron is connected to only a few neurons in the previous layer, unlike fully connected networks. <L[09L1-cnn] 10><L[09L1-cnn] 11><L[09L1-cnn] 12>
\textbf{Parameter Sharing<L[09L1-cnn] 12>}: A technique used in convolutional neural networks where the same set of weights (parameters) is used across all spatial locations in a feature map. <L[09L1-cnn] 12>
\textbf{Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)<L[09L1-cnn] 13>}: A piecewise linear activation function defined as $f(x) = \text{max}(0, x)$.  It is commonly used in neural networks due to its computational efficiency and ability to avoid the vanishing gradient problem. <L[09L1-cnn] 13>
\textbf{Max Pooling<L[09L1-cnn] 14><L[09L1-cnn] 15>}: A pooling operation that selects the maximum value within a defined region (e.g., 2x2) of a feature map. <L[09L1-cnn] 14><L[09L1-cnn] 15>
\textbf{Average Pooling<L[09L1-cnn] 15>}: A pooling operation that calculates the average value within a defined region (e.g., 2x2) of a feature map. <L[09L1-cnn] 15>
\textbf{Backpropagation<L[09L1-cnn] 16>}: An algorithm used to train neural networks by calculating the gradient of the loss function with respect to the network's weights and updating the weights accordingly. <L[09L1-cnn] 16>
\textbf{Convolutional Kernel Layer<L[09L1-cnn] 17>}: A layer in a convolutional neural network that performs the convolution operation, applying filters to extract features from the input data. <L[09L1-cnn] 17>
\textbf{Dimension Reduction Layer<L[09L1-cnn] 17>}: A layer in a convolutional neural network that reduces the spatial dimensions of the feature maps, typically using pooling operations. <L[09L1-cnn] 17>
\textbf{Fully Connection Layer<L[09L1-cnn] 17>}: A layer in a neural network where each neuron is connected to every neuron in the next layer. <L[09L1-cnn] 17>
\textbf{Learned Convolution Filters<L[09L1-cnn] 18>}: The weights of the convolutional filters in a convolutional neural network that are learned during the training process.  These filters detect specific features in the input data. <L[09L1-cnn] 18>

Modeling Systematic Biases in Recommender Systems: $r_{ij} \approx \mu + b_i + b_j + u_i \cdot v_j$, where $r_{ij}$ is the rating, $\mu$ is the overall mean rating, $b_i$ is the user bias, $b_j$ is the item bias, and $u_i \cdot v_j$ represents user-item interactions.<L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 44>

Root Mean Square Error (RMSE): $\frac{1}{|R|} \sum_{(u,i) \in R} (r_{ui} - \hat{r}_u)^2$, where $R$ is the set of ratings, $r_{ui}$ is the actual rating, and $\hat{r}_u$ is the predicted rating.<L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 49>
K-means Clustering:  The algorithm iteratively assigns data points to the nearest cluster centroid, then recomputes the centroids as the mean of the points in each cluster, repeating until convergence. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 22>

Euclidean Distance: $d_E(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{p} (x_i - y_i)^2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are $p$-dimensional vectors. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 17>

Hamming Distance: Counts the number of differing bits between two binary vectors. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 19>

Matching Coefficient:  Hamming distance normalized by the number of attributes/bits. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 19>

Purity: $purity(C, G) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{K} \max_{j} N_j \in G_i$, where $N$ is the total number of data points, $K$ is the number of clusters, and $N_j$ is the number of points of class $j$ in cluster $i$. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 44>
DPLL Algorithm: A backtracking-based algorithm for solving the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT). It systematically assigns truth values to variables, checking for contradictions and backtracking when necessary. <L[13L1-Logic] 15><L[13L1-Logic] 16><L[13L1-Logic] 17><L[13L1-Logic] 19><L[13L1-Logic] 24>

Conversion to CNF: A set of rules to transform any logical expression into an equivalent Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) expression.  This is crucial for using SAT solvers, as many solvers are designed to work specifically with CNF. <L[13L1-Logic] 17><L[13L1-Logic] 18>
Recursive Fibonacci: $fib(n) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n \le 1 \\ fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$<L[14L1-DepthFS] 6>

Recursive Binary Search Tree Search:  Recursively check the current node's value ($V$) against the target value ($X$). If $V == X$, return `True`. If $X < V$, recursively search the left subtree; if $X > V$, recursively search the right subtree. If no children exist, return `False`.<L[14L1-DepthFS] 10>

Breadth-First Search: Explore nodes level by level, adding children to a queue.<L[14L1-DepthFS] 8>

Depth-First Search: Explore a branch completely before moving to another branch.<L[14L1-DepthFS] 8>

Optimized Fibonacci (Dynamic Programming): Store previously calculated Fibonacci numbers in a cache to avoid redundant computations.<L[14L1-DepthFS] 23>
Naïve\_SAT: A recursive algorithm that explores all possible variable assignments to determine the satisfiability of a propositional formula. It checks for immediate satisfiability or unsatisfiability, then recursively calls itself with assignments of true and false to an unassigned variable, backtracking if both fail.<L[15L2-SAT] 18>

DPLL: A recursive algorithm that improves upon the Naïve\_SAT algorithm by incorporating Boolean Constraint Propagation (BCP) to efficiently identify and resolve unit clauses, significantly reducing the search space.<L[15L2-SAT] 17>

BCP: A sub-algorithm within DPLL that repeatedly identifies and assigns values to literals in unit clauses (clauses with only one unassigned literal), creating a cascading effect that simplifies the formula and often leads to quicker conflict detection.<L[15L2-SAT] 20>

Resolution Rule: An inference rule that derives a new clause from two existing clauses containing a literal and its negation.  The new clause combines the remaining literals from the original clauses using logical OR.<L[15L2-SAT] 32>

Clause Learning: A technique used to learn from conflicts encountered during the DPLL search.  When a conflict occurs, a concise reason (a clause) is learned to prevent similar conflicts in the future, improving efficiency.<L[15L2-SAT] 35>

Hamiltonian Path Encoding:  A method to encode the Hamiltonian Path Problem into a SAT problem.  It uses Boolean variables $h_{ij}$ representing whether the $i$-th vertex visited is vertex $j$.  Constraints are added to ensure the path uses only existing edges and visits each vertex exactly once.<L[15L2-SAT] 46>

Graph Coloring Encoding: A method to encode the Graph Coloring Problem into a SAT problem.  It uses Boolean variables to represent the assignment of colors to vertices, with constraints ensuring that adjacent vertices have different colors.<L[15L2-SAT] 47><L[15L2-SAT] 48><L[15L2-SAT] 49>
Fairness through Blindness: Ignore protected attributes during model training and prediction. <L[16L2-ethics] 25>

Group Fairness: $P(\text{outcome } o | S) = P(\text{outcome } o | T)$, where $S$ and $T$ are two groups.  This is insufficient as a fairness metric. <L[16L2-ethics] 26>

Individual Fairness: Treat similar individuals similarly; similar individuals should have similar outcomes.  How to achieve this is an open research question. <L[16L2-ethics] 27>

Detecting and Removing Bias from Models: Keep bias features in the data during training, then remove what was learned from these features after training. <L[16L2-ethics] 34>
